summary: Teach the immune system (ages 9–11) as the body's layered DEFENCE against germs (bacteria and viruses): first the skin as a barrier keeping germs out, then white blood cells that patrol inside and find and destroy germs that get in, and finally vaccines that safely TRAIN the body in advance to recognise a specific disease. The organising ideas are 'layers of defence' and that the body can learn and remember an enemy, which is why a vaccine given now protects later. Anchor in experience (a scab sealing a cut, feeling unwell while fighting infection, why we get jabs) and connect white blood cells to the cells–tissues–organs hierarchy (cells with a defence job). Keep it qualitative; named cell types, antibodies, and the innate/adaptive split belong to later study. The central misconception to fix is that medicines/antibiotics are the same as the body's own immune defence, and the counter-intuitive idea to land is that a vaccine trains rather than cures or infects.
misconceptions: 'Medicine/antibiotics do the fighting' — rather than the body's OWN immune system doing the defending.
'Vaccines give you the disease' — they use weakened/inactive germs or pieces to train the body safely.
'Vaccines cure a disease you already have' — they prevent by training in advance, not treat after.
'Germs are all the same' — missing that bacteria and viruses are different kinds of invader.
'The skin is just a covering' — missing its role as the first line of defence (a barrier).
'Once germs are in, nothing can stop them' — missing the active role of white blood cells.
'Being unwell means the body is losing' — symptoms often show the immune system actively fighting.

activities.title: Defend the body: barrier, defenders, and the vaccine comparison
steps: Watch or help as germs swarm the skin barrier and a few slip through; follow the white blood cells patrolling the blood as they chase down and destroy the germs inside.
Run the infection first with NO vaccine: notice the body struggles and takes a long time to win.

Then give a vaccine first — a harmless 'practice' germ (or part of one) that the white blood cells learn to recognise — and run the SAME infection again; observe the defenders recognise the real germ much faster and defeat it, in this model before illness sets in (in real life a vaccine usually prevents the illness or makes it milder, but not always).
Compare the two runs side by side and state in your own words what the vaccine did (and did not do).
Open the myth-flap 'Does the jab make me sick?' and explain why the practice germ is safe.
activities.insight: Immune defence is an active process in layers: the skin is a barrier, white blood cells actively hunt and destroy germs inside, and a vaccine does not fight the disease for you or give it to you — it trains your own body in advance so the real germ is defeated faster.

activities.title: Reveal the layers of defence
steps: Tap or lift each layer in turn: the skin barrier outside, then the white blood cell defender patrolling inside, then the vaccine 'training card'.
Describe what each layer does in its own words before revealing the explanation.
Lift the flap on 'Does a vaccine give you the illness?' and say why the answer is no.
activities.insight: The body defends in distinct layers with different jobs — barrier (skin), active defence (white blood cells), and prevention by training in advance (vaccines).

activities.title: Consolidate: order, match, and judge
steps: Sequence the layers of defence: barrier (skin) → white blood cells inside.
Match each component to its job (skin → keeps germs out; white blood cell → finds and destroys germs; vaccine → trains the body in advance).
Judge true/false statements that target vaccine and medicine misconceptions, e.g. 'A vaccine gives you the disease', 'Medicine, not your body, does the fighting' or 'Antibiotics cure any germ'.
Judge true/false statements about the cause and types of germs, e.g. 'You catch a cold just from being cold, not from germs' and 'Bacteria and viruses are exactly the same kind of germ'.
activities.insight: Learners can recall and distinguish the roles of barrier, defender cells, and vaccine, reject common vaccine myths, and recognise that infectious illness is caused by germs — with bacteria and viruses being different kinds of invader.

activities.title: Ask the doctor about vaccines (optional companion)
steps: Pose questions such as 'Why do I need a jab if I feel fine?' or 'Why doesn't the vaccine make me ill?'
Ask the follow-up 'Why might I need a booster later?' and restate what a booster does.
Read the factual reply and restate the 'train in advance' idea in your own words.
activities.insight: A vaccine is given when you are well because its job is to train your defences in advance, not to cure or to infect you; a booster is a reminder dose that re-trains the body if its 'memory' of the germ fades over time.

checkQuestion: A vaccine is made from weakened or inactive germs, and you get it when you are NOT sick. How can putting a bit of a germ into a healthy person PROTECT them from that disease later? And why doesn't the vaccine give them the disease?
checkAnswer: The vaccine shows the immune system a harmless version (weakened, inactive, or just a piece) of the germ, so the white blood cells learn to recognise and 'remember' it — without the person getting ill, because the germ in the vaccine is too weak or inactive to cause disease. If the real, dangerous germ arrives later, the immune system already recognises it and destroys it fast, before it makes the person sick. The vaccine trains the body's own defences in advance.
